The paper develops a two-fluid model (TFM) for heat transfer in dense non-Brownian suspensions.
The TFM includes separate mass, momentum, and energy conservation equations for the particle and fluid phases.
The rheological model for the particle phase includes shear and bulk viscosities, as well as an anisotropic stress term.
The proposed inter-phase heat transfer coefficient is a function of the shear rate, particle volume fraction, and particle and fluid thermal properties.
The paper provides a conceptual explanation for 'thermo-rheological' particle migration forces arising from temperature-dependent fluid viscosity.
Simulations show that both shear and thermal gradients can drive particle migration, with the direction depending on their relative orientation.
The maximum packing fraction of the particles is taken to be 0.68, corresponding to close-packed spheres.
The calibrated values of the parameters in the inter-phase heat transfer coefficient are β = 0.2 and m = 1.
The paper validates the TFM against heat pulse experiments in a Couette cell and qualitatively against data for an eccentric Couette cell.
The energy equations in the TFM neglect viscous dissipation and the effect of buoyancy, as these were found to have marginal effects.
The paper aims to provide a general and extensible computational framework for simulating the interaction between heat transfer and particle migration in dense suspensions.
Applications of interest include geothermal energy recovery, hydraulic fracturing, hemodynamics, microfluidics, electronic cooling, and food processing.
The TFM does not make the equilibrium assumption between the fluid and particle phases, unlike traditional single-phase suspension balance models.
The paper highlights the importance of capturing the inter-phase heat transfer and the coupling between thermal and shear gradients in dense suspension flows.
The geometric eccentricity of the Couette cell can be used to tune the thermal performance of the suspension flow.
